reply_text:
㊥ (gist) Recorded (futon2 `d8c85edf8`): shares-patterns and unblocks are two tokens with different semantics — `@how` generalised and `@why` generalised — and the Cascade Live–based simplified cascade is the outer driver. B1's number is the `@how` one; the centrality you mean is the `@why` one, and no source holds it at HEAD, so I added B1b to find what could.

㊣ ("those have different semantics") Yes, and the two directions already carry the distinction in claude-17's §7: `@why` is the pattern's own author saying what the pattern answers, read *upward* to say why an unmet pattern matters; `@how` is an editor naming the methods, read *downward*. For items: "X unblocks Y" means Y's `@why` points at X — Y goes from unanswered to answered when X completes — and "X shares patterns with Y" is that both reach for the same methods. The first is dependency; the second is coupling. B1 measured coupling (ρ 0.896 with the live occurrence count, so the click's current "centrality" is coupling too).

㊭ (B1b, next discovery after B2's amendment returns) Three candidate sources for an inter-item `@why`, kept apart: (i) cross-references in the 107 documents to other M-/E-/T- ids, each classified by the cue around it (`depends on`, `blocked by`, `feeds`, `prerequisite`, `see`) and cited by line; (ii) any lifecycle field that names a predecessor or consumer; (iii) the library's 545 `why` edges lifted to items through applied patterns, reported as a *derived* relation only. Plus a one-paragraph proposal for how an item would *declare* what rests on it (`cascades/declared-skeleton`: declare only what you would defend in review) — a derived relation being at best a prompt for a declaration. B3 then pastes in an `unblocks-reading` square that emits a typed absence until the relation exists, and a separate `shares-patterns` square whose token is consumed only if you want coupling scored at all.

㊢ (in flight) codex-33 is on the B2 amendment (job `invoke-1791243056763-33300-48dcabb4`, park `park-91999bb4`): operator share restricted to post-hook commits, with the headline being how many of the 107 have any attributable history.

previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) Written: `futon2/holes/E-aif-cascade.md` (futon2 `987898239`), the excursion that codex-33 works through item by item instead of waiting on packets from me. It records what is done today, then three sections of work with an acceptance bar per item: A, the R-nodes as a cascade (discovery → your ruling on the cut → Lean receipt → drawing → each R-unit read as a blend square); B, elaborating the outer-loop diamond with the two requirements you named; C, the causal reading and a chain comparison that is actually between constructible things. codex-33's A1 job has just finished; its wake has not reached me yet, so I will review it in the next turn.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: ("centrality" and "feasibility" — where they stand) Centrality is already in the loop twice, in different forms: it is the live selector's *only* scored channel (`1/(1+occurrence count)` on the Cascade Live map — that is what chose `M-interim-director-proxy-metric-inventory`), and it is in the diamond's outcome vocabulary as `downstream-unblocking`. Feasibility is there once each side: the live selector's `:automated-feasibility` support filter, and the diamond's machine-side `injury` arm. **Operator-turn load is in neither.** So B1/B2 are discoveries of the two tokens (what "unblocks the most" means per task kind, citing claude-4's rows measure rather than recomputing it; the share of an item's recent touches that were operator turns), B3 pastes the two squares into the diamond as the blend reading requires — centrality consumed by the generative model's `downstream-unblocking` term, operator load either as a support change like `injury` or as a preference term, both written up for you to choose — as an edn diff and a receipt, and B4 measures whether the extension changes the ranking of the real run against the live selector's, under `E-outer-loop-improvement`'s ablation rule.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: ("the reward for the bag, that's a bit unfortunate") Less so than it looks: the bag is not an arrangement the tokens admit — `fill` fires before the observation exists — so a constructed cascade never offers it, and the scorer only produced the number because it was handed the edge list. What the measurement does show is that a per-step C with no consumption rule would reward it if it were offered, which is C3's item: charge the token emitted with no consuming want. And yes — each requirement added is one more square with its own token, and the picture stops being describable as anything but a cascade; B3's receipt will make that literal (meets, linear extensions) rather than a claim.

previous_reply_acts.text: (how the excursion runs) codex-33 takes the next unchecked item in its section; every item ends in a commit and a bell with the sha; I review (record, test adequacy, selective re-execution) before the next starts; your rulings — A2 the cut, B3 support-change vs preference, B5 promotion of `meta/select-the-meta-item`, and the two v3 decisions — are recorded in the note when given. Sections A and B can run on two seats if you want a second one minted; C1 waits for claude-17's page.
